figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: A Hexel is a planar patch with a soft hexagonal boundary; together, Hexels approximate a 3D surface (left). Its center \bp, orthogonal unit tangents \btu,\btv, and scales $s_{u},s_{v}$ determine its position, orientation, and size (center). Color varies linearly from \bc0 at the center, with RGB gradients \bgu,\bgv along local coordinates $u,v$. $K$ (spatial weight) controls the patch’s influence: increasing sharpness $\beta$ sharpens the boundary (right). The tileable hexagonal support and local linear color field jointly exploit structure in scene geometry and appearance, allowing each Hexel to represent larger coherent regions while retaining a controllably sharp boundary.

abstract: Novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction have advanced rapidly with radiance fields and splatting, yet their memory and computational demands limit their use in resource-constrained settings. We introduce Hexels: novel planar hexagonal surface elements with a first-order spatial color field for efficient 3D scene and 2D image representation. Hexels exploit locally planar regions with smoothly varying appearance using fewer, larger primitives. Their hexagonal support provides an area- and boundary-efficient domain, while the local color field captures appearance variation within each primitive. Across 34 scenes, Hexels improve PSNR over memory-matched 2DGS by 4.53–7.38 dB across datasets while requiring lower training VRAM. We further ablate Hexels by showing that per primitive, Hexels outperform 2DGS by upto 4.74 dB while using lower training VRAM and having $2.31\times$ faster FPS. Even in unconstrained settings, Hexels offers complementary quality-memory trade-offs. For efficient 3D surface reconstruction, Hexels reduce error by 28.9% compared with memory-matched 2DGS across 15 DTU scans. On 6 Tanks and Temples surface scenes, Hexels achieves the highest mean F1 among compared methods (34.38%, versus 31.72% for 2DGS). We further also show that Hexels, as a general primitive, improves 2D image representation over Image-GS. Hexels push the Pareto frontier on the quality-efficiency trade-off of surface-aligned primitives.

sections.body: The introduction says existing methods add per-primitive textures or neural appearance fields, which move complexity into other components. Hexels are planar hexagonal surface elements with a first-order color field, so one primitive can cover a locally planar region with smooth color variation. At matched model sizes, the paper reports PSNR gains of 4.53–7.38 dB over 2DGS, with up to 3.6× less VRAM. For surface reconstruction, mean Chamfer distance is 0.978 mm versus 1.375 mm for memory-matched 2DGS. The paper also reports faster convergence and better 2D image representation than Image-GS.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing surface primitives need many overlapping elements for smooth regions, so this paper proposes one hexagonal primitive with a first-order color field.

sections.body: The related work groups prior methods into redesigned kernels (Triangle Splatting, Deformable Beta Splatting, 3D Convex Splatting), hybrid methods that move appearance into textures or neural fields (BBSplat, NeST, Nexels), and retrofits such as pruning, quantization, distillation, or baking. The section states that the first two groups raise memory, training VRAM, or computation. Hexels are presented as general surface primitives that apply to oriented 3D surfaces and to 2D images without major changes to the representation or optimization. The section names five axes: storage, training VRAM, primitive count, FPS, and reconstruction quality.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior methods add memory through heavier kernels, textures, or neural fields, so this paper redesigns the primitive itself.

sections.body: Each Hexel is a planar patch with a center, two orthogonal tangent directions and two tangent scales, mapping local coordinates (u, v) to 3D. Its support is a sigmoid of a hexagonal distance d(u, v), with a learned sharpness beta that sets the edge width. Color is a base RGB value plus two RGB gradients along u and v, so the color varies linearly within the patch. The paper states that under a first-order approximation a suitably oriented hexagon can cover about 30% more area than a square for the same bounded color error. Rendering reuses the 2DGS ray-plane intersection and front-to-back compositing. V2 adds a linear view-dependent residual and V3 uses degree-three spherical harmonics.
sections.heading: Hexels: Hexagonal Surface Elements
sections.headline: A Hexel pairs a soft hexagonal support with a linear color field, using 20 learned parameters in its view-independent form.

sections.body: The section evaluates 9 Mip-NeRF360 scenes, 15 DTU scans and 10 Tanks and Temples scenes against 3DGS, 3D Convex Splatting, BBSplat, Nexels, 2DGS, Triangle Splatting and MeshSplatting, using PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, training time, peak training VRAM, FPS and deployment size. Table 2 reports matched model memory, where the caption says Hexels achieves the best PSNR and SSIM across all three benchmarks. Table 3 reports matched primitive budgets, with PSNR gains over 2DGS of up to 4.74 dB. An ablation on a planar target with 256 primitives gives 37.07 dB for the linear-gradient Hexel versus 35.13 dB for the Gaussian with the same appearance model.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: On 34 scenes, Hexels reach higher PSNR than 2DGS at matched memory and at matched primitive budgets.

sections.body: The conclusion reports PSNR gains of up to 7.38 dB at matched model memory and rendering up to 2.31× faster than 2DGS. The section states that a first-order color model cannot represent arbitrary texture within one primitive, that sparse initialization can leave parts of a scene poorly covered, and that the surface cells do not form a watertight mesh. Sharper footprints do not by themselves prevent sampling artifacts at small projected sizes or grazing views. Hexels do not outperform every baseline on every metric. Developable Hexels, curved patches with zero Gaussian curvature, are proposed as future work.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Hexels establish a quality–efficiency frontier among evaluated surface primitives, but a first-order color cannot model arbitrary texture.

sections.body: Appendix A gives the parameter counts, support and color derivatives, and optimization coordinates. Appendix B covers perspective-correct ray-plane coordinates and support bounds that use an alpha threshold of 1/255. Later sections list fixed and densified results (Table 14, Table 15), lossless and PQ1024 compression with quality changes relative to uncompressed models (Table 16), and 2D model sizes. Appendix J gives per-scene V3 densified results (Tables 17 to 19), and Appendix K shows additional qualitative comparisons in Figures 13 to 15.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers parameterization, derivatives, rasterization, compression, and per-scene and qualitative results.
